passage: The bus to the village was late and rain drummed on the roof, but Sachin, nine, kept his face against the window the whole way. At his grandmother's farm he jumped into the mud in his new sandals. "It's like chocolate!" he shouted. His cousin Neelam, fourteen, laughed and handed him a mango from the basket. He ate three, juice running down his elbows. He chased the calf. At five the next morning he woke and saw Neelam already coming back from the well with two buckets, her feet caked with the same mud. She tipped the water, then sat down to cut fodder. "Don't you play?" he asked. "After the work," Neelam said, smiling. Sachin sat quietly with the peel of his mango.

qa.q: What did Sachin say the mud was like?
qa.a: Sachin shouted, "It's like chocolate!"

qa.q: How does Sachin feel at the farm on the first day, and how might that change the next morning?
qa.a: At first Sachin is thrilled and joyful. The next morning he seems thoughtful and quiet, since he sees Neelam doing the work he had thought was play.

qa.q: What turning point made Sachin sit quietly with his mango peel?
qa.a: He saw Neelam back from the well with two buckets at dawn and heard her say she would play after the work, showing him the effort behind the farm.

qa.q: What might Neelam's mornings be like, and how does she seem to feel about them?
qa.a: Busy with chores like fetching water and cutting fodder. She smiles and says "After the work," so she seems used to it and comfortable.

grounding: A city child on a village holiday is thrilled by mud and mangoes and begins to see the hard work behind the simple life.

passage: Back in their Mumbai flat, Vinita, eight, dumped her muddy sandals by the door and told her mother about the whole holiday, talking faster than she could breathe. "Mud, and mango trees, and Mohit took me to see the buffaloes!" She showed the photo of Mohit standing next to a calf. Her mother listened, then said, "Mohit gets up before sunrise to help with the milking, beta, before he goes to school." Vinita paused. "Before school?" "Every day." Vinita looked at the photo again. Mohit was smiling, but his sleeves were rolled and his hands looked rough. "I thought it was all playing," she said slowly. "Can I send him my crayons?" Her mother nodded.

qa.q: What did Vinita tell her mother about the buffaloes?
qa.a: Vinita said that Mohit took her to see the buffaloes.

qa.q: How does Vinita feel at first, and how does she feel after hearing about the milking?
qa.a: At first Vinita is excited and joyful. After she hears about the milking she is thoughtful and caring, and wants to send Mohit her crayons.

qa.q: What choice did Vinita make after learning about Mohit's mornings?
qa.a: Vinita asked if she could send Mohit her crayons, choosing a kind gesture instead of dropping the idea that it was all playing.

qa.q: What might Mohit's days be like?
qa.a: He gets up before sunrise to help with the milking and then goes to school, so his days are full of work as well as fun.

grounding: A city child on a village holiday is thrilled by mud and mangoes and learns about the hard work behind the simple life.

passage:
"Nilesh Mama, why are you awake? It's still dark!"
"Cows don't wait for the sun, Rashmi. Want to come?"
"Yes!"
"Put on the slippers. There's mud."
"Mud! I love mud!"
"You'll love it less at four in the morning every day."
"Is this every day? Even Sunday?"
"Every day. Even Diwali."
"Oh." ...
"Here, hold the bucket. Gently."
"She's so warm! And look at the mango trees! Mama, you're so lucky. It's so peaceful here. I wish I lived here."
"Peaceful, yes. Also, the rains came late this year and half the paddy dried up."
"Then what happens?"
"Then we work harder, and hope next year is better. Now, carry this bucket back without spilling."

qa.q: What time does Mama say the cows need him?
qa.a: He says, "You'll love it less at four in the morning every day."

qa.q: What was Rashmi feeling when she said she wished she lived there?
qa.a: Rashmi felt thrilled and happy, excited by the mud, the warm cow and the mango trees.

qa.q: What could help Rashmi see the village more fully?
qa.a: Listening to Nilesh Mama about the late rains and the daily work, and helping with chores, could teach her about the hard work behind the peace.

qa.q: How might Nilesh Mama feel when Rashmi calls him lucky?
qa.a: He might feel amused and a little tired, loving his life but aware of how hard it is when the rains fail.

grounding: A city child visiting a village is thrilled by mud and animals, while an adult hints at the hard work behind the simple life.

passage:
When I was ten, Mummy sent me to our village near Nashik for the whole summer. I'm Sumit, and I thought it was going to be the best holiday of my life.
It was. I climbed mango trees and swam in the canal. I told my cousin Ritu, who's my age, "You're so lucky, you don't even have to study!"
She looked at me strangely.
The next day I woke up early and saw her. She was carrying water from the well before school, then feeding the goats, then walking three kilometres to school. In the evening she helped cook, then did homework by a small lamp.
I felt stupid. I'd thought her life was all mangoes.
I'm fourteen now. I still love that village. But I understand it better.

qa.q: How far did Ritu walk to school?
qa.a: Ritu walked three kilometres to school.

qa.q: What did Sumit feel when he saw Ritu's day?
qa.a: Sumit felt stupid and embarrassed, realising he had imagined her life as all mangoes.

qa.q: What could Sumit do differently on his next visit?
qa.a: Sumit could help Ritu with her chores and ask about her day, instead of assuming village life is easy.

qa.q: How might Ritu have felt when Sumit called her lucky?
qa.a: Ritu probably felt surprised and a bit hurt, since her days were full of hard work he hadn't seen.

grounding: A city child loves a village holiday and first romanticises it, then learns of the hard work behind the simple life.

passage:
Camp coordinator's note, school farm-stay, Day 3.
Arohi, ten, from our Bengaluru batch, has been the happiest child on this trip. She runs barefoot in the fields and told me today, "I want to live here forever. No traffic, no homework!"
This morning she followed Pooja, the farmer's daughter, who is her age, to the fields at six. Pooja showed her how to pull weeds. After twenty minutes Arohi's back hurt and her hands were scratched.
She came back quiet. "Pooja does this every day before school," she told me. "And she still has homework."
I didn't give a speech. I asked her what she'd learned. She said, "It's beautiful here, but it's hard."
Next step: I've asked Pooja and Arohi to make a poster together for the group on "A Day on the Farm."

qa.q: How long did Arohi pull weeds before her back hurt?
qa.a: After twenty minutes Arohi's back hurt and her hands were scratched.

qa.q: What does Arohi coming back quiet suggest she felt?
qa.a: It suggests she felt surprised and thoughtful, maybe a little humbled, after seeing how hard Pooja works.

qa.q: Why was it wise for the coordinator not to give a speech?
qa.a: Asking Arohi what she learned let her put the lesson in her own words: the village is beautiful but hard.

qa.q: How might Pooja see Arohi's visit?
qa.a: Pooja might find it funny or touching that Arohi wanted to live there forever, and feel proud to show her real work.

grounding: A note shows a city child thrilled by farm life who learns, by working beside a village child, about the hard work behind it.

passage:
Hafsa's holiday diary, Day 3.
Best day EVER. Rajni took me to the mango orchard and we ate three each, juice running to our elbows. I stepped in mud up to my ankle and lost a slipper, and Rajni laughed so hard she sat down. The buffalo is called Rani. She breathes like a pressure cooker.
Everything here is slow. Nobody is in a hurry. I told Nani I want to live here forever.
One thing was strange. Rajni had to get up before it was light to carry water from the handpump, and she couldn't come to the pond after lunch because she had to cut fodder. She said, "You're lucky, you're a guest." I didn't know what to say.
Tomorrow we are making mango pickle. I will ask if I can carry water too.

qa.q: What is the buffalo called?
qa.a: The buffalo is called Rani.

qa.q: What was Hafsa feeling in the orchard, and what shows it?
qa.a: Hafsa felt thrilled and carefree, calling it the best day ever and eating mangoes with juice running to the elbows.

qa.q: What could Hafsa do to understand village life better?
qa.a: Hafsa could ask Rajni about her mornings and actually help with the water, as planned, to see the work behind the slow, sunny days.

qa.q: How might Rajni see Hafsa's holiday?
qa.a: Rajni may feel a little tired or envious, since Hafsa gets to play while she carries water and cuts fodder, which shows in "You're lucky, you're a guest."

grounding: It illustrates a city child thrilled by mud, mangoes and a slower rhythm in a village, with first hints of the hard work behind it.
